summary: Hearthy is our answer to the FieldShift challenge. It uses open NASA and ESA satellite data to detect crop disease early, starting with soybean Sudden Death Syndrome, with a proof of concept in Iowa. The farmer outlines a field and enters the planting date, and Hearthy analyses every new satellite pass for signs of stress. What makes it different is that it separates disease from other causes such as hail, flooding, drought or natural maturity, so farmers get an alert only when disease is the likely cause. Instead of raw data, farmers receive a clear weekly status, a quick plan for confirming disease in the field, and a map for targeted treatment next season. By showing where disease keeps coming back, Hearthy helps farmers choose healthier, more resilient crop rotations, which is the goal of FieldShift. Farm data stays private, and the tool supports the farmer’s judgment rather than replacing it.
details:
What it does and how it works
Hearthy detects crop disease early using open satellite data, starting with soybean Sudden Death Syndrome (SDS), with a proof of concept in Iowa. A farmer outlines a field and enters the planting date. Hearthy then analyzes each new satellite pass, using Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2 imagery harmonized through NASA’s HLS product, and tracks vegetation and moisture indices (such as NDVI, EVI and NDMI) against the expected pattern for that planting date. Weather and crop-rotation data help the system separate disease from other causes of stress, including hail, flooding, drought and natural maturity. Farmers receive an alert only when disease is the likely cause.

Benefits and intended impact
Instead of raw data, farmers get a clear weekly status, a short plan for confirming disease in the field, and a map for targeted treatment next season. Because SDS appears in patches and is hard to spot on foot, this saves scouting time and reduces unnecessary fungicide use. By showing where disease keeps coming back, Hearthy helps farmers choose healthier, more resilient crop rotations, which is the goal of FieldShift. Because it relies on free, open data, it can scale to other crops and regions at low cost.

Tools and technology
[Google Earth Engine / Python / other, fill in what you used], NASA HLS, Landsat 8/9, Sentinel-2, [weather source such as PRISM or gridMET], and USDA’s Cropland Data Layer for crop history. [Add front-end, hosting and any machine-learning tools you used.]

What makes it creative
Most tools show vegetation health. Hearthy goes one step further by asking why a field is stressed, and speaks to the farmer in plain language rather than in data layers.

Factors we considered

  • Cloud cover: we mask clouds and shadows and combine several satellites to maximize usable images. If no clear image is available in a given week, Hearthy says so instead of assuming the field is healthy.
  • Resolution: at 10 to 30 meters, the system works best for patches rather than individual plants.
  • Privacy: farm data stays private.
  • Farmer judgment: the tool supports the farmer’s decisions rather than replacing them, and always recommends confirming in the field.
